title: Filter all employees whose salary is greater than 50,000.
shortTitle: Filter all employees whose salary is greater than 50,000

s1_definition.profdef: `Stream.filter(Predicate)` is an intermediate stream operation that keeps only the elements for which the supplied predicate returns `true` and discards the rest. It is lazy, so nothing happens until a terminal operation such as `collect` runs, and it returns a new stream rather than mutating the source collection.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has a list of all its employees. The HR manager stands at the door with one rule in her head: "Only let through the people who earn more than 50,000." Rajesh earns a lot and walks through; a junior clerk earning 30,000 is stopped. `filter` is exactly that door with a yes/no rule.
s1_definition.oneliner: `filter` keeps the elements that pass a true/false test and throws away the rest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Stream.filter(Predicate)` is an intermediate stream operation that keeps only the elements for which the supplied predicate returns `true` and discards the rest. It is lazy, so nothing happens until a terminal operation such as `collect` runs, and it returns a new stream rather than mutating the source collection.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has a list of all its employees. The HR manager stands at the door with one rule in her head: "Only let through the people who earn more than 50,000." Rajesh earns a lot and walks through; a junior clerk earning 30,000 is stopped. `filter` is exactly that door with a yes/no rule.

**One line to remember:** `filter` keeps the elements that pass a true/false test and throws away the rest.

sections.s2_technical:
A stream is a pipeline of operations over a sequence of elements. The `filter` method takes a `Predicate<T>`, which is a functional interface with a single method `boolean test(T t)`. Because it has exactly one abstract method, you can pass a lambda such as `e -> e.getSalary().compareTo(new BigDecimal("50000")) > 0`.

For money we always compare with `BigDecimal.compareTo` and never with the greater-than sign on a double, because floating point loses precision and a bank can never afford a rounding error on salary or balance. `compareTo` returns a negative number, zero, or a positive number, so greater than zero means strictly greater than fifty thousand.

`filter` is lazy and returns a `Stream<T>`. You can chain many filters, and the stream engine fuses them so each element is tested once as it flows through, not once per filter pass. For example `stream.filter(e -> e.isActive()).filter(e -> e.getSalary().compareTo(limit) > 0)` reads each employee a single time.

A senior nuance: `filter` does not modify the original list. The source `List<Employee>` is untouched; you get a brand new result from the terminal `collect(Collectors.toList())`. This immutability is valuable in banking where the master employee list must stay authoritative.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants to run its annual bonus cycle. Finance says only employees earning more than 50,000 a month are eligible for the senior bonus pool. HR has one flat list mixing everyone from the tea-stall contractor to senior engineers like Rajesh. Someone has to pull out just the high earners without disturbing the master list. This is exactly how `filter` works — it reads every employee, applies the single rule "salary greater than 50,000", and produces a fresh shortlist while the original record stays safe.

The code will define an `Employee` class with name, department, gender, age, email and a `BigDecimal` salary. A `PayrollService` class will hold a method `highEarners(List<Employee>)` that streams the list, applies the salary predicate, and collects the survivors. A small runnable `Main` builds a sample list including Rajesh and Priya and prints the eligible employees with a logger.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four employees — Rajesh (95000), Priya (72000), Amit (48000), Sunita (exactly 50000).

Step 1: `staff.stream()` opens a pipeline over the four employees. Nothing is computed yet; the stream is lazy and just waiting.

Step 2: The terminal `collect` pulls the first element, Rajesh. The predicate tests 95000 compared to 50000 — the result is positive, so Rajesh passes through.

Step 3: Priya flows in. 72000 compared to 50000 is positive, so Priya passes.

Step 4: Amit flows in. 48000 compared to 50000 is negative, so Amit is dropped and never reaches the result.

Step 5: Sunita flows in. 50000 compared to 50000 is zero, which is not greater than zero, so Sunita is also dropped because the rule is strictly greater than.

Step 6: `collect(Collectors.toList())` gathers the survivors Rajesh and Priya into a brand new list. The original `staff` list is untouched.

```
    │
    ▼
  stream()                      (lazy pipeline opens)
    │
    ▼
  filter(salary.compareTo(50000) > 0)
    ├─ Rajesh 95000  → +ve → PASS ─┐
    ├─ Priya  72000  → +ve → PASS ─┤
    ├─ Amit   48000  → -ve → DROP  │
    └─ Sunita 50000  →  0  → DROP  │
                                   ▼
  collect(toList())  →  [Rajesh, Priya]   (new list; source unchanged)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Filtering a stream means keeping only the elements that satisfy a condition and discarding the rest. In Java 8 I open a stream with the stream method on my collection, then call filter and pass a predicate, which is just a function that returns true or false for each element. The engine tests every element against that predicate and only the ones that return true survive into the result, which I materialize with a terminal operation like collect.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this during the annual bonus cycle. I had one master list of employees and finance needed only those earning more than fifty thousand a month for the senior bonus pool. I streamed the list and filtered with a predicate that compared each salary against the threshold. Crucially, because salary is money I compared using the BigDecimal compareTo method and checked that the result was greater than zero, never using a floating point greater-than operator, because in a bank even a tiny rounding error is unacceptable.

A senior point I always add is that filter is lazy and non-destructive. It builds a pipeline that does nothing until a terminal operation runs, and it never modifies the original list — it returns a fresh collection. That immutability matters because the master employee record must remain the single source of truth while I derive as many filtered views as I like. I can also chain several filters, and the stream fuses them so each employee is examined exactly once as it flows through the pipeline, which keeps it efficient even on large datasets.

---

keyPoints: Uses filter() with a Predicate<T> to select matching elements
Lazy operation — no processing until terminal operation
Can chain multiple filters or use complex Predicate with && ||
